title: A generic ERC-4626 adaptor lets Spark onboard any compliant vault without new controller code
content:
The Fluid sUSDS instance declares that it "follows the general ERC4626 procedures" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.5.1.3) and the process definitions use address-parameterised functions: `function depositERC4626(address token, uint256 amount) external onlyRole(RELAYER) isActive` (.5.1.3.1.1), `withdrawERC4626(address token, uint256 amount)` (.5.1.3.2.1) and `redeemERC4626(address token, uint256 shares)` (.5.1.3.2.5.3). The underlying asset is discovered at runtime — `IERC20 asset = IERC20(IERC4626(vault).asset())` — rather than configured.

Because the vault address is an argument, one code path serves every ERC-4626 venue. Onboarding Fluid required no new controller function; contrast the Aave and Ethena paths, which needed protocol-specific entry points (`depositAave`, `prepareUSDeMint`, `cooldownAssetsSUSDe`).

The consequence is that the standard's ubiquity becomes Spark's attack surface. Any address implementing `deposit`/`withdraw`/`redeem` is callable through the same function, including a malicious vault that accepts an approval and never honours redemption. Nothing in the code path distinguishes Fluid from an arbitrary ERC-4626 impostor.

That is precisely why the whitelist-by-rate-limit design is load-bearing here rather than merely convenient: the generic adaptor removes every other place a venue check could live. Governance's control over which vaults Spark can touch reduces, entirely, to which (action, vault) keys have a non-zero limit.
description: depositERC4626, withdrawERC4626 and redeemERC4626 take the vault address as a parameter, so the venue-specific logic collapses into configuration
